body: I'll have to look into this - debugging on StackBlitz is not viable as the Service Worker there messes with the way the network error flows through.

I noticed an additional (and devastating) behavior in the latest chrome: You can cancel a request using the ctrl+s shortcut (which opens a save dialog). This makes it stupidly easy to break an angular website which relies on the completion of an observable to show / hide loading messages. This can for example also break the angular.io website by simply hitting ctrl+s while switching to a new page (simulating a slow network makes the timing easier). I know that most users don't spam ctrl+s, but I still think this issue should be investigated / prioritized.
Got the same issue. Could anyone provide an information regarding to it?

body:
Seems like we figured out where is the problem. 

We fallowed the same steps @PascalHonegger provided: make a pending request and put laptop into sleep mode. 

We tested it by creating two requests: one through simple **XMLHttpRequest** and another one through Angular **HttpClint**. We subscribed on HttpClint and all XMLHttpRequest events. As was discovered cancelation of request triggers abort event on XMLHttpRequest. We dived deeper and found that HttpClient listens to only three events: _progress_, _load_ and _error_. 

That is why Observable never ends. XMLHttpClient returns an abort but Angular doesn't react on it.

We made a small fix on our side just adding an **HTTP_INTERCEPTOR** which cancels a request if it doesn't respond after 1 min. But we also made a PR to Angular to support this event (#28338).

We also suffer a lot because of this issue. If user has unstable network and application send a series of requests, then it is impossible to know if request was canceled or server is polling requests.
Handling of _abort_ event is very required in HttpClient
@vladjerca That makes sense to me.  No reason for it to be an error, we just need *some* way to tell that it happened.

@vladjerca Yes, probably, it should not be an error. But anyway some notification should appear in such case. Now we have the total silence from the HttpClient and also there is no information about such behavior in documentation. So many developers can get unexpected bug when they will deal with unstable network connections.
This is a huge problem, I am surprised it hasn't been fixed yet.

I don't think this should be labeled as `freq1:low`.
It happens every time in my case if I quickly click login / action / action... / logout in my app.
I'm a developer of https://github.com/cyclosproject/cyclos4-ui.
The app has a global HTTP interceptor, which knowns when there are pending requests (https://github.com/cyclosproject/cyclos4-ui/blob/master/src/app/core/api.interceptor.ts). As a fallback, after 15 seconds the request is removed from the pending queue.
In the following video you can see that after logging-in, clicking a bunch of actions and logging out, the login button is disabled, and gets re-enabled after a few seconds. That means that the notification for request completion was never generated for some requests...
![Angular - canceled http requests](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1183737/59764452-3125d200-9272-11e9-837f-b4a6ec79ea11.gif)

PS: I've now applied a workaround, so every page component clears the request queue. But internally there are still missing requests.

So is there a workaround or not right now? 

@vladjerca Is this something I can implement in my code or is it just a demonstration of what Angular can do to fix this problem?

Same usecase, same error nearly two years later.

As requests are cancelled by chrome, my loading spinner won't disappear.
